paperReadings.note: The course publishes no slides publicly, so its course material is the per-lecture paper reading list on the site. Lecture 2's four readings (all CC BY 4.0) are transcribed in raw/papers/ from their arXiv LaTeX sources: Large Language Monkeys in full including its appendix; How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?, Snell et al. and Archon main body only (appendices left at arXiv to save budget). Lecture 3's readings: only Weaver (Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers) is CC BY 4.0 and is transcribed, main body only; Cobbe et al. 2021, Lightman et al. 2023 and Math-Shepherd carry arXiv's non-exclusive licence and are linked and discussed in the wiki, not transcribed. Lecture 4's three readings (ReAct, RLEF, Constitutional AI) are all CC BY 4.0 and transcribed main body only. Lecture 5's five readings: LATS and SWiRL (CC BY 4.0) are transcribed main body only; SPRINT (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), ADaPT and Wider or Deeper? (arXiv non-exclusive) are linked and discussed, not transcribed. Lecture 6's three readings (STaR, DeepSeekMath, DAPO) all carry arXiv's non-exclusive licence and are linked and discussed in the wiki, not transcribed. Lecture 7's three readings: AlphaCode (Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode) is transcribed main body only, relying on its arXiv CC BY 4.0 listing although the PDF prints an all-rights-reserved notice; the AlphaCode 2 Technical Report (all rights reserved) and Search-o1 (arXiv non-exclusive) are linked and discussed, not transcribed. Lecture 8's three readings (Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks, GDPval, DeepScholar-Bench) are all CC BY 4.0 and transcribed main body only, in the versions current on the lecture date: METR's arXiv v2 and DeepScholar-Bench's v1 (both since revised), and GDPval's v1 (its only version). Lecture 1 lists no readings. PDFs are not committed; every paper is cited at its original URL (sources.md).

caveats: PARTIAL: covers catalog lectures 1 (Course Overview), 2 (Test-Time Compute Scaling), 3 (Robust Verification), 4 (Learning from Feedback with Tools/Code), 5 (Planning and Multi-Step Reasoning), 6 (Train Time Scaling/Scaling RL), 7 (Self-Improvement and Deep Research Agents) and 8 (Agentic Evaluations and Long Horizon Tasks) of 9. Do not cite this KB as covering CS329A as a whole.
Lecture 1 is transcript-only: the course publishes no slides and the site lists no paper readings for it.

Lecture 2's readings: three of the four (power laws, Snell et al., Archon) are transcribed main body only; their appendices are not in this KB. Lecture 2 shows two charts that are not in the transcribed text — a SWE-bench chart with a DeepSeek model the lecturer believes was DeepSeek-V3 (not in any reading) and Archon's fusion/ranking win-rate chart (in its appendix) — so those passages are cited to the transcript only.
No KB-written figure descriptions exist: the chat must not read values off a figure image; quote the caption and the paper's text.

The auto-captions garble some model and benchmark names in lecture 1's Large Language Monkeys results (about 22:34-25:42) and a term in its reasoning-model steps (about 32:00); in lecture 2 the Archon optimizer's name ('itest', about 47:23) and a percentage from a manual answer check (about 26:08). These are marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcripts and not restored from outside knowledge.
Lecture 2 states Archon's average improvement as 14.1%; the paper's abstract reports 15.1% (over o1, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet). The wiki gives both.

Lecture 3's readings: three of the four (Cobbe et al. 2021, Lightman et al. 2023, Math-Shepherd) are arXiv non-exclusive licence and are NOT transcribed; the wiki cites them by section, figure and table at their arXiv URLs, and has no images of them. Weaver is transcribed main body only.

Lecture 3 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: the lecture gives Weaver-at-70B as 86.2% (paper Table 3: 87.6%) and the distilled verifier as keeping 97% of accuracy with 99%+ less compute (paper: 98.2%, or 98.7% in its abstract, and 99.97%); it describes Lightman et al.'s 'convincing wrong-answer' samples as having correct final answers, where the paper defines them as reaching incorrect ones; and its claim that majority voting generalises better than the ORM holds in Lightman et al.'s Table 1 on the three AP exams but not on AMC10/12 or in aggregate.
Lecture 3's captions leave two words unclear, marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcript and not guessed: a term in a student question at about 16:25 and one at about 35:08 (likely 'hacking').

Lecture 4's three readings (ReAct, RLEF, Constitutional AI) are transcribed main body only; their appendices, which hold the prompts, the constitution's principles and further ablations, are not in this KB.

Lecture 4 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: the lecturer says ReAct's thoughts are separate from the action space, where the paper's formalism puts them in an augmented action space; it glosses WebShop's score as covering intermediate steps, where the paper defines it by the attributes of the product chosen; and it glosses RLEF's n@k solve rate differently from the paper's definition. RLEF's own text gives the 70B model's test-set result as 38.0 where its Table 1 lists 40.1. A chart shown at about 46:50 (fine-tuning with and without RLHF across model sizes) has method names the captions garble, so the wiki does not tie it to a figure.

Lecture 5's readings: LATS and SWiRL are transcribed main body only. SPRINT (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) and ADaPT and Wider or Deeper? (arXiv non-exclusive) are NOT transcribed and have no images; the wiki cites SPRINT by section, figure and table, and summarises ADaPT and Wider or Deeper? from their abstracts only, because the recording does not discuss them.

Lecture 5 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: it describes LATS's LM and self-consistency scores as added together, where the paper weights them with a hyperparameter; reflection as generated after success or failure, where the paper reflects on unsuccessful trajectories; and the paper as not analysing cost, where the version consulted (ICML 2024) has a sample-complexity and token-consumption analysis. It calls LATS's WebShop results close to human experts, which holds for the score (75.9 vs 82.1) but not the success rate (38.0 vs 59.6). LATS's HotPotQA experiments use an oracle that reports whether an answer is correct. The DeepSeek-R1 training curves shown at about 24:19 are not from any reading.

Lecture 5's captions leave some words unclear, marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcript and not guessed: the benchmark named on the DeepSeek-R1 training curves (about 24:19), a word in the contrast with Math-Shepherd (about 5:37), a word at about 15:40, and 'fork' twice (about 20:21 and 34:29).

Lecture 6's readings (STaR, DeepSeekMath, DAPO) all carry arXiv's non-exclusive licence: they are NOT transcribed and have no images; the wiki cites them by section, figure, table and equation at their arXiv URLs.

Lecture 6 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: it places DeepSeekMath's 51.7% (and about 60% with further tricks) on AIME, where the paper reports 51.7% and 60.9% on MATH and gives no AIME score; it quotes STaR at 51.7%, which is not a STaR result; it attaches generalized advantage estimation to GRPO, where the paper uses GAE in PPO and replaces it with a group baseline; and it describes DAPO's 47-point comparison as DeepSeek-R1 distilled into Qwen 32B, where the paper's is DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B, RL on the base model.

Lecture 6's captions leave some words unclear, marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcript and not guessed: the reasoning-model names at about 7:52, a word before the 72.5% accuracy at about 30:28, two words in a distillation question at about 33:35, a method for updating fewer weights at about 50:47, the kind of score asked about at about 51:32, the name of DeepSeek's 47-point model at about 53:06 (the DAPO paper's comparison is DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B) and a phrase at about 1:07:43. At about 41:27 the captions give no name for a PaLM-based STEM paper, and none is supplied.
Lecture 6's closing figures on the share of RL versus pre-training in frontier models (including a Grok 4 claim) are the lecturer's recollection, not from any reading.

Lecture 7's readings: AlphaCode is transcribed main body only on the strength of its arXiv CC BY 4.0 listing, although its published PDF prints '© 2022 DeepMind. All rights reserved'. The AlphaCode 2 Technical Report (all rights reserved) and Search-o1 (arXiv non-exclusive) are NOT transcribed and have no images; the wiki cites them by heading or section, figure, table and equation. The lecture's asides on Search-R1, 'Agentic Context Engineering' and model calibration are not from any reading.

Lecture 7 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: it introduces AlphaCode's GOLD as a regularization technique, where the paper's regularizer is tempering and GOLD is an offline RL training objective; it describes AlphaCode 2's family of models as varying by difficulty level and tags and its dataset as segmented, where the report varies hyperparameters and randomizes ratings and tags at sampling time; it calls the updated CodeContests open source and says AlphaCode 2's scoring model was trained on a higher-quality, human-annotated dataset, neither of which the report states; it first says Search-o1 is competitive with human experts in physics and chemistry, then corrects to physics and biology (Table 2: behind chemists on chemistry, 40.7 vs 72.6); it says standard RAG typically improves on direct reasoning, where the Search-o1 paper finds it does not effectively address knowledge gaps; and it says Search-o1 reduces uncertainty-word counts, which the paper's text does not state for Search-o1.

Lecture 7's captions leave some words unclear, marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcript and not guessed: a word at about 27:29, a phrase about researchers at about 33:51, a student's question at about 35:23, a phrase at about 36:57 and a word at about 40:06; speaker turns are best-effort in four exchanges (about 11:01, 20:30, 35:23, 53:17). 'About 50 case samples' (about 29:06) is kept as captioned; the AlphaCode 2 report gives about 50 thousand candidates after filtering.

Lecture 8's readings are transcribed main body only, and two of them from earlier arXiv versions: METR's Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks from v2 (30 March 2025) and DeepScholar-Bench from v1 (27 August 2025), the versions current on the lecture date and the ones the lecture quotes. Both have since been revised with different numbers and names (METR v3/v4, retitled '...Long Software Tasks'; DeepScholar-Bench v2, which renames DeepScholar-base), and their arXiv abstract links serve the latest version. Figure, table and section numbers in this KB follow the transcribed versions.

Several lecture 8 numbers come from GDPval's appendix, which is not transcribed: the 1.6x cost and 1.4x speed gains for GPT-5, the severity of GPT-5's lost tasks, win rates by sector and task duration, the under-contextualized-prompt experiment, the roughly $400 mean task value and the 89% well-specified rate. The wiki cites them by appendix section. The occupations the lecture names as at or near expert level (about 42:18-45:25) are the lecturer's readings of appendix charts.

Lecture 8 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: the captions give the 80% time horizon as 'five weeks shorter' where METR says about 5x shorter; it adds training-data contamination to METR's explanation of SWE-bench's shorter doubling time; it describes GDPval's sectors as the 'top 5% of the GDP' and its digital filter as 60% of O*NET tasks, where the paper selects sectors each contributing over 5% of U.S. GDP and occupations whose tasks are at least 60% digital; it attributes a 'less than 10% of the human expert salary' cost figure to the GDPval discussion that is a METR finding; it describes DeepScholar-Bench as spanning 22 domains at PhD-level difficulty and re-run monthly, where v1 gives 18 arXiv domains and a plan to continuously re-run; and it describes METR's 50% success rate as an average of per-task success rates, where the paper fits a logistic curve per model.

Lecture 8's captions leave some words unclear, marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcript and not guessed: a source of higher-value tasks at about 34:32 ('cvLancer'), a benchmark at about 50:05 ('ML-Bench'), 'the beta paper' at about 1:11:16 and 'five weeks shorter' at about 22:03; speaker turns are best-effort in five exchanges (about 0:51, 9:29, 21:17, 24:19, 31:20).
